newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: ACT NZ says policies would deliver lower dollar.
newsitem.headline: ACT NZ says policies would deliver lower dollar.

text.p: The free-market ACT New Zealand Party said on Wednesday its policies would deliver a lower New Zealand dollar by cutting government spending.

Speaking at the launch of the party's manifesto in Wellington, leader Richard Prebble said government price rises, such as ACC charges, were the major cause of inflation, which in turn was keeping the dollar high.
"Inflation causes the higher dollar and inflation is a government problem," Prebble said.
He said the policies of opposition New Zealand First, which is competing with Labour for second place in opinion polls, were already adding 1.5 percent to two percent to interest rates.
ACT's bottom line for the October 12 election would be the continuation of the current economic direction.
"ACT is only prepared to compromise on the speed of reform but never the direction," Prebble said.
He ruled out a coalition deal with the left wing Alliance, economic nationalist New Zealand First and "the present Labour Party".

"Only National has the economic policies to be in government. However I do not have any real confidence that National would guard the inheritance they were given in 1990," Prebble said. National took office in 1990 after defeating Labour.
Prebble said National's position that it would do deals on the Reserve Bank Act and the Employment Contracts Act showed it could "easily be drawn back into old-time socialism".
He said he was concerned Prime Minister Jim Bolger had not ruled out deals with any party after the election.
"The founders of National would turn in their graves at the thought of a deal with the Alliance. I don't find that credible and neither does the Alliance," Prebble said.
He said a handful of ACT MPs in parliament would see the introduction of a funded superannuation scheme because there was probably a majority in the current National government that agreed with one.
ACT wants to introdue a flat tax rate of 19.5 cents in the dollar of which seven cents would be placed in a private superannuation scheme of the taxpayer's choice.
It also wants eduation funding tied to students, not institutions, and competition in the health sector, with government funding for universal private "catastrophic" health insurance.
Prebble said the only policy ACT was likely to share with a Labour-New Zealand First-Alliance govenrment was the abolition of the superannuation surcharge.
ACT is averaging 3.8 percent in recent polls and needs five percent to be certain of seats in parliament unless Prebble can win the Wellington Central seat.

He is polling a close third to National's Mark Thomas and Labour's Alick Shaw, but a rebel group in National are pressing Thomas to withdraw to ensure Prebble wins and delivers a coalition partner for National. Thomas has said he will stay in the race.
Prebble was a minister in the last Labour government but lost his Auckland Central seat in the 1993 election to Alliance deputy leader Sandra Lee.
He became ACT leader earlier this year after its founder, former Labour Finance Minister Roger Douglas, stepped down.
